MARKET.head: Australian wine exports fall 7% as US and China weaken, Canada and Southeast Asia rise
MARKET.summ:
Australian wine exports declined overall in the year ending September 2026, but the results varied significantly across markets. Strong growth in Southeast Asia and Canada was offset by more challenging conditions in the United States (US). 

This Market Bulletin will analyse the latest export data, released...
takeaways: Australian wine exports fell 7% in value to $2.25 billion in the 12 months to September 2026, with volume down 5%.
Exports to the US dropped 28% in value to $219 million, the biggest driver of the volume decline.
Canada grew 12% in value to $185 million as American wines were pulled from shelves in the trade dispute, while Southeast Asia rose 16% to $291 million.

MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads fine wine trade at 39.6% of value, Lafite top
MARKET.summ: Bordeaux led the market, claiming 39.6%, Lafite accounting for over a quarter of its trade
takeaways: Bordeaux held the lead in fine wine trade with 39.6% of traded value, with Lafite accounting for over a quarter of it.
Burgundy fell from 24.8% to 18.4% of traded value, while Tuscany rose from 5.2% to 8.9%.
Bollinger overtook Dom Perignon and Louis Roeder as the top-traded Champagne producer by value.

MARKET.head: VinePair's weekly roundup covers Supreme Court case, Uncle Nearest sale, and more
MARKET.summ: This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Diageo’s toxic chemical spill, SCOTUS to review a home distilling case, the latest product releases, and more.
takeaways: The Supreme Court will review a home distilling case, according to VinePair's weekly roundup.
Fawn Weaver has moved to block a sale of Uncle Nearest, with potential buyers also reported.
Southern Glazer's faces a bribery snafu, and OpenTable published a 2026 restaurant report.

CULTURE.head: Navarra's demanding rosé methods become a premium signal, a model for English wine
CULTURE.summ: How Navarra Rosado turned production challenges into premium positioning and a compelling marketing story. Andrea Ontiveros Flores, a sommelier and marketing & communications specialist from Alicante, Spain asks if English wine could do the same? Consumers rarely pay more simply because winemaking is difficult.
takeaways: Navarra rosado has moved from cheap everyday wine to a premium category, with the region producing rosé alongside Provence.
Producers use the Saignée method, which can need up to three times more grapes than standard red wine production.
The D.O. Navarra Regulatory Council introduced a Rosado Tradition designation requiring Saignée and exclusive Garnacha use.

CULTURE.head: Real Housewives drink mass-market, sweet wines, shaped by Parker-era taste
CULTURE.summ: What do the reality stars’ drinking habits reveal about wealth, taste, status and the economics of the U.S. wine industry?
takeaways: Real Housewives cast members mostly drink mass-market, high-alcohol, sweet California cabernets, according to essayist Cake Zine contributor.
Essayist links this taste to Robert Parker's 100-point system, which rewarded fruit-forward, higher-alcohol wines from 1978 onward.
Mary Cosby of Salt Lake City praised the 2003 Dom Pérignon, a vintage ripened sweet by a heatwave that killed 5,600 people.

CULTURE.head: Cloudy, unfiltered pét nat wines gain ground on UK supermarket shelves
CULTURE.summ:
There’s something refreshing about unfiltered or unfined wines. We filter through a selection …

Centuries ago, Geoffrey Chaucer observed that “ther is no newe gyse that it nas old”. This truth - that there is nothing new under the sun - certainly applies to wine: every year, a well-documented or ancient viticultural...
takeaways: Marks & Spencer's Trouble, a cloudy organic rosé, is the first cloudy still wine sold in a British supermarket, per the column.
Pét nat is bottled before fermentation finishes and usually left undisgorged, which gives it a cloudy look.
Ottolenghi's house wines are unfiltered and cloudy, with Zainab Majerikova saying the haze adds texture and suits big-flavoured food.

SCIENCE.head: UK vineyards navigate early, hot, dry 2026 harvest after frosts
SCIENCE.summ: After a run of dramatically different vintages, 2026 has given UK viticulture another season that challenged assumptions, but also demonstrated just how much English and Welsh vineyards can achieve. The 2026 growing season began with a series of extraordinary frost events, creating a challenging start before developing into a...
takeaways: 2026 began with a series of extraordinary frost events, then turned warm, dry and rapidly ripening across English and Welsh vineyards.
Harvest arrived several weeks early at some sites, while dry weather kept disease pressure manageable and fruit arrived clean.
Growers now face heat stress and water availability alongside traditional cool-climate problems, pushing decisions toward fruit monitoring rather than the calendar.

SCIENCE.head: Domaine Bousquet details organic and water-saving practices at its Mendoza winery
SCIENCE.summ: Domaine Bousquet continues to elevate Argentine wine through generations of dedication and innovation in organic wine practices. Earlier this year, Irma Remigio and her team warmly welcomed SWR’s Membership Manager, Ilva Fridenberga, to their winery. The winery, located at the foot of the Andes Mountains, is globally recognized...
takeaways: SWR membership manager Ilva Fridenberga visited Domaine Bousquet's Mendoza winery at the foot of the Andes in February.
The winery is trialling biodiversity and garden vineyard corridors, harvesting from outside the rows where natural vegetation is left undisturbed.
It switched to high-pressure hoses for cleaning harvest boxes after comparing water use, and is a signatory of the Bottle Weight Accord, targeting still bottles under 420g.

SCIENCE.head: MODIS satellite data estimates vineyard water use in Italy's Veneto region
SCIENCE.summ: In North-Eastern Italy water demand for vineyards irrigation is constantly increasing, but this conflicts with the high civil and industrial rates of water consumptions in the area, which is one of the most densely populated in Europe
takeaways: Padova University researchers developed a Remote Sensing method using MODIS satellite data to map vineyard evapotranspiration regionally.
The model was calibrated on two years of eddy-covariance measurements from a 25-hectare vineyard in northeastern Italy and tested on two independent years.
Estimates showed good consistency with in situ observations, suggesting MODIS could monitor vineyard water use at regional scale.

SCIENCE.head: Newick Wine Estate in East Sussex hit by 2026 frost, despite planting 37,000 vines
SCIENCE.summ: Newick Wine Estate in East Sussex is a place of outstanding tranquillity. Newick Village is situated almost equal distance from both Canterbury and Winchester, two important Cathedral cities in the south of England. It is not surprising therefore that the village has an ancient history.
takeaways: Jonathan and Charlotte Sharpe planted 37,000 vines on half of their 16-hectare East Sussex farm at Newick Wine Estate in 2023.
Ten frost events hit the vineyard in 2026, four causing significant damage, with the final one on 10 May.
The team is using monitoring traps, dead-end hosts and bio-diversity measures to control spotted wing drosophila (SWD) pests.

SCIENCE.head: Portuguese trial cuts vine yields with Ethephon and manual thinning in two grapes
SCIENCE.summ: Some years, climate conditions and biological events increment the fertility of vines, which can lead to over cropping and a decrease of wine quality
takeaways: A 2007 trial in Vinhos Verdes tested Ethephon, Prohexadione-calcium and manual bunch thinning on Loureiro and Borraçal vines.
Manual bunch thinning cut Borraçal yield by about 41% and Loureiro yield by about 26% against control.
Ethephon applied at berry buck-shot size cut Loureiro yield 35%, while earlier application cut Borraçal yield 70%.

SCIENCE.head: Grenache rootstocks and irrigation shape water use and stomatal control in Spain
SCIENCE.summ: Under the context of global change, any decrease in water use by crops is essential, because water is becoming a more and more scarce resource, especially in Mediterranean areas, where grapevines are grown
takeaways: Irrigation trial in a three-year-old Spanish Grenache vineyard compared three rootstocks, 110-R, 41-B and 161-49C, under irrigated and non-irrigated regimes.
Water use efficiency was higher in non-irrigated vines, and higher on 110-R and 41-B than on 161-49C.
Stomatal conductance differences from irrigation persisted through the season, and the authors suggest hormonal signals matter more than hydraulic ones.

SCIENCE.head: Italian researchers propose climate-adaptive grape breeding and local variety conservation strategies
SCIENCE.summ: In the globalization conditions possible future scenarios, optimistic and pessimistic are supposed
takeaways: Authors argue grapevines will need genotypes more resistant to biotic and environmental stress as growing areas shift.
Italian regions have started safeguard projects to recover abandoned local grape varieties and preserve genetic biodiversity.

SCIENCE.head: Conegliano pruning trials on Lazio grape varieties assess yield, quality and marketing
SCIENCE.summ: In this work the salient results of the viticultural and ecomomic researches earned out on interesting italic varieties of Latium (Malvasia of the Lazio and Cesanese d'Affile) and an international vsriety (Cabernet sauvignon), "Cordon Spur of Conegliano" (CSC) as growing system, will be exposed
takeaways: CRA Conegliano and Lazio research bodies trialled Cordon Spur of Conegliano on Malvasia di Lazio, Cesanese d'Affile and Cabernet Sauvignon.
Researchers compared Vertical Tridimensional Minimal Pruning of Conegliano with and without DMRC double maturation to raise gross saleable product.
Work aims to limit overcropping and conserve water, a growing concern for Mediterranean vineyards under climate change.

SCIENCE.head: Growers Use Specialist Machinery to Cut Winter Vineyard Labour
SCIENCE.summ: As autumn turns to winter a list of jobs looms large in the calendar. The vines need pruning and the soil needs care and attention. To make these jobs less demanding and costly, different tools can be used.
takeaways: Winter vineyard jobs include pruning and soil care, which growers can make less labour-intensive with specialist tools.
Cordless battery secateurs and a tractor-mounted pre-pruner speed up pruning, the latter cutting away tendrils to ease cane removal.
Mechanical sweepers gather canes into a row so a flail mower can mulch prunings in the same pass, while frost tools include wind machines and Ventigel.

SCIENCE.head: English and Welsh vineyards report earliest harvests on record in 2026
SCIENCE.summ: Record-early starts, ripe and healthy fruit, and a season that kept teams on their toes. Spring frost left its mark on some, but the mood across the industry is one of real excitement. As I look back to last year’s report of earliest on record, 2026 seemed in a hurry to beat it.
takeaways: Gusbourne in Kent began picking Pinot Noir on 26 August 2026, two weeks ahead of 2025.
Nyetimber in West Sussex began its earliest ever harvest on 14 September, five days ahead of its 2018 record.
Spring frosts in Hampshire cut yields at The Grange and Black Chalk, though fruit quality was reported as high.

SCIENCE.head: Vine balance: how growth and fruiting trade off across the season
SCIENCE.summ: Vine balance is a commonly used term in viticulture that expresses the concept of an appropriate balance of vegetative to reproductive growth of the vine
takeaways: Vine balance describes the proportion of vegetative growth to reproductive growth in grapevines, a concept hard to quantify directly.
A balanced vine ripens its crop, develops fruitful buds for next year, and builds reserves without excessive canopy growth.
Simulation models of carbohydrate production can track seasonal growth demands against canopy carbon supply.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Cantina Terlarno and Produttori del Barbaresco: an amazing dinner with two of the world’s great cooperative wineries, tasting back to the 1960s
NEWSLETTERS.summ: I was very happy to attend this dinner! Held by the excellent Fine + Rare at Wiltons, the evening featured
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Fine + Rare hosted a dinner at Wiltons featuring 25 wines from Cantina Terlano and Produttori del Barbaresco, with bottles going back to the 1960s.
Cantina Terlano, founded in 1893 in Alto Adige, sources from about 200 families across 1,500 parcels, with average yields of 49 hl/ha.
Produttori del Barbaresco is a small cooperative of 53 farmers farming 120 hectares solely with Nebbiolo, and began making single-cru Barbaresco in 1967.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Vinography Images: Fire in the Forest
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Fall colors at the Pintas vineyard in Portugal’s Douro Valley decorate the ancient stone terraces surrounded by greenery. In the
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow
takeaways: Vinography published an image feature titled "Fire in the Forest" showing fall colors at the Pintas vineyard in Portugal's Douro Valley.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Marion Granges-Faiss runs Domaine de Beudon, a six-hectare vineyard at 890 metres in Valais, Switzerland, reachable only by cable car or a steep hike.
Jacky Granges-Faiss bought the estate in 1971; after his death in June 2016, Marion became the de facto winemaker.
Beudon's wines ferment on the mountain but are aged and bottled at Pierre-Antoine Crettenand's winery in Saillon, and most contain added sulphites.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Nasty Not Nice
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Why are people drinking less, when wine is better than ever? I have an idea. Wine is too good.
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Tim Atkin argues wine is too pleasant and reassuring, and that the trade should inject insecurity and difficulty to attract buyers.
He notes that wine sales rose when cork taint affected one in four or five bottles, and are now declining.
He suggests bottling each barrel separately and running Bordeaux en primeur sales like Smithfield's unsold-meat auction, to create excitement.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Inside Chinon’s Lieux-Dits Project
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Vignerons lead a collective effort to recognize the vineyards behind the appellation’s Cabernet Francs
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Chinon's lieux-dits project, begun by the Chinon Syndicat in 2014, aims to promote vineyard heritage without a formal hierarchy or INAO classification.
Seven lieux-dits have been officially recognized so far, starting with La Croix Boissée in Cravant-les-Côteaux in 2018.
Each recognized lieu-dit is documented in a monograph and marked by an engraved stone, with Matthieu Baudry of Domaine Bernard Baudry on the working group.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Yet Another Vintage Port Flex Post (Tasting Selections From 1985 - 2022)
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Last week, I published a bunch of reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the (stellar) 2024 Port vintage. I typically follow those type of posts up with another post of other, older selections of vintage Ports that I tasted at the same event, and I offer them without much shame as simply […] This article was...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Joe Roberts
takeaways: 1WineDude published reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the 2024 Port vintage.
A follow-up post covers older vintage Ports tasted at the same event, spanning 1985 to 2022.

NEWSLETTERS.head: N is for Noirien
NEWSLETTERS.summ: What eco-geotypes tell us about grape genetics, geography, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Noirien is an old French word for Pinot noir, derived from Latin niger, meaning black or dark.
The Noirien group includes Pinot noir and its color mutants, plus Chardonnay, Gamay noir, Auxerrois, Melon and Troyen.
Noirien's zone runs from Champagne through the Côte d'Or to Beaujolais, and from the central Loire east to Alsace and the Jura.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Why Michelin Ratings Still Won’t Tell You Who Actually Made Your Burgundy Wine
NEWSLETTERS.summ: This wine guide explains why no critic's score, not even from a renowned guide like Michelin, truly reveals who made your regional wine. Consumer insight is key
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: Since July, a growing number of Burgundy bottles carry Michelin ratings of one to three grapes, assessed on five criteria: agronomy, technical mastery, identity, balance and consistency.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Telling a mountain to move
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Delving into the details of change in the DO Montsant wine region of Catalunya
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: DO Montsant, in Catalunya's Priorat area, has revised its bylaws to add certification for vi brisat, its orange-style wine.
Montsant's revised bylaws also create a classification for 'minimal intervention' wines, including mandatory hand-harvesting and organic certification.
The minimal intervention rules require spontaneous fermentation, no oenological additives except gentle filtration, and a sulfur dioxide limit far below conventional levels.

NEWSLETTERS.head: 400 Montepulciano Bottles for Thomas Jefferson circa 1805
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine everyone’s been gushing over since the middle ages!
NEWSLETTERS.author: Eveline Chartier
takeaways: A 1350 trade contract between the Del Pecora family and merchant Jacopo di Vanni is the oldest known document for Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.
A 2024 document from the Consorzio del Vino Nobile di Montepulciano dates the first known use of the term 'Vino Nobile' to 1766, by the Jesuits.
Thomas Jefferson received 473 bottles of Montepulciano in November 1805 and requested 400 more bottles annually, per his April 1806 letter to Thomas Appleton.
